message.abstract: <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title><jats:p>Let <jats:italic>f</jats:italic> be an edge ordering of <jats:italic>K</jats:italic><jats:sub><jats:italic>n</jats:italic></jats:sub>: a bijection <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="graphic/rsa20592-math-0001.png" xlink:title="urn:x-wiley:10429832:media:rsa20592:rsa20592-math-0001"/>. For an edge <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="graphic/rsa20592-math-0002.png" xlink:title="urn:x-wiley:10429832:media:rsa20592:rsa20592-math-0002"/>, we call <jats:italic>f</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>e</jats:italic>) the label of <jats:italic>e</jats:italic>. An <jats:italic>increasing path</jats:italic> in <jats:italic>K</jats:italic><jats:sub><jats:italic>n</jats:italic></jats:sub> is a simple path (visiting each vertex at most once) such that the label on each edge is greater than the label on the previous edge. We let <jats:italic>S</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>f</jats:italic>) be the number of edges in the longest increasing path. Chvátal and Komlós raised the question of estimating <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>n</jats:italic>): the minimum value of <jats:italic>S</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>f</jats:italic>) over all orderings <jats:italic>f</jats:italic> of <jats:italic>K</jats:italic><jats:sub><jats:italic>n</jats:italic></jats:sub>. The best known bounds on <jats:italic>m</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>n</jats:italic>) are <jats:inline-graphic xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink" xlink:href="graphic/rsa20592-math-0003.png" xlink:title="urn:x-wiley:10429832:media:rsa20592:rsa20592-math-0003"/>, due respectively to Graham and Kleitman, and to Calderbank, Chung, and Sturtevant. Although the problem is natural, it has seen essentially no progress for three decades.</jats:p><jats:p>In this paper, we consider the average case, when the ordering is chosen uniformly at random. We discover the surprising result that in the random setting, <jats:italic>S</jats:italic>(<jats:italic>f</jats:italic>) often takes its maximum possible value of <jats:italic>n</jats:italic> – 1 (visiting all of the vertices with an increasing Hamiltonian path). We prove that this occurs with probability at least about 1/ <jats:italic>e</jats:italic>. We also prove that with probability 1‐ <jats:italic>o</jats:italic>(1), there is an increasing path of length at least 0.85 <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>, suggesting that this Hamiltonian (or near‐Hamiltonian) phenomenon may hold asymptotically almost surely. © 2015 Wiley Periodicals, Inc. Random Struct. Alg., 48, 588–611, 2016</jats:p>
title: Increasing Hamiltonian paths in random edge orderings
